The arrow operator is a postfix operator, like (), [] and the dot, so it binds tighter than every prefix operator such as ++, --, *, & and a cast. That fixes the meaning of the combinations that appear in output questions: ++p->x increments the member, (++p)->x moves the pointer first, p++->x reads the member of the current record and then moves, and *p->q dereferences a pointer member. The address of member m of record i is computed from the base address, the record size and the member offset, which is why p + 1 always jumps over a whole record, padding included.

Passing a structure by value copies all of it, including any array member, so a function can change its copy without the caller noticing; a bare array argument, by contrast, always decays to a pointer. An array of structures passed to a function also decays to a pointer to its first record, so the function works on the caller's records. A function may return a structure by value, even one built on the spot with a C99 compound literal such as return (struct P){x, y};, but a returned pointer must point to storage that outlives the call: heap memory, a static object or a record in the caller's array.

theoryAdd.text: In output questions, first decide for each call whether it receives a copy (a struct T parameter) or an address (struct T *, or an array of structures). Only the address forms can change the caller's records, and a pointer parameter that is itself reassigned inside the function does not change the caller's pointer.

questions.questionText: Given struct Emp { int id; char name[20]; float sal; } e[50];, assume int and float are 4 bytes and 4-byte aligned (no padding is needed, because every member already starts at a multiple of 4). How many bytes does the array e occupy?
questions.explanation: One record is 4 + 20 + 4 = 28 bytes (sal starts at offset 24, so there is no padding). The array holds 50 records: 50 × 28 = 1400 bytes.

questions.explanation: %d needs the address of the int member, &s[i].roll (the & applies to the whole s[i].roll). name is an array, which already converts to the address of its first character, so it takes no &. s[i] is a structure, not a pointer, so -> is wrong, and the array s itself has no members.

questions.questionText: Given struct P { int x; } arr[3]; and struct P *p = arr + 1;, which expression does NOT refer to arr[2].x?
questions.explanation: p[1], *(p + 1) and *++p all denote the record after arr[1], i.e. arr[2]. In p++->x the post-increment yields the old value of p, so it reads arr[1].x (p moves to arr[2] only afterwards).

questions.questionText: For struct Big { double d[100]; int n; };, assume double is 8 bytes and 8-byte aligned, int is 4 bytes and pointers are 8 bytes. How many bytes are copied into the parameter when a struct Big is passed by value, and when its address is passed instead?
questions.explanation: The members need 800 + 4 = 804 bytes, rounded up to a multiple of 8 (the alignment of double): sizeof(struct Big) = 808, all of which is copied by value. Passing the address copies only a pointer, 8 bytes.

questions.questionText: Why is a function often declared as void print(const struct Student *s) rather than void print(struct Student s)?
options: A structure cannot be passed by value in C
const makes the function run at compile time
Passing a pointer gives the function a private copy of the record
Only an address is copied instead of the whole record, and const stops the function from modifying the caller's record
questions.explanation: Passing by value is legal but copies sizeof(struct Student) bytes on every call. A pointer copies only an address, and const gives the same protection a copy would, because the compiler rejects writes through s.
An array of structures passed to a function decays to a pointer to its first record, so bump changes the caller's elements to 2 and 3. bumpOne receives a copy of arr[0], so its increment is lost.

options: Compile error: a member cannot be selected from a function result
questions.explanation: make(3) returns {3, 9}, whose x is 3; make(4) returns {4, 16}, whose y is 16. A member of a returned structure can be selected directly with the dot operator.

options: Compile error: a function cannot return an array
questions.explanation: The parameter s is a copy of x, array included, so doubling s.a leaves x.a unchanged (x.a[2] = 3). The modified copy is returned into y, so y.a[2] = 6. Wrapping an array in a structure is a way to pass and return it by value.

questions.questionText: struct P { int x; }; is defined and <stdlib.h> is included. Which function returns a pointer that the caller can safely use after the call (ignore allocation failure)?
options: struct P *f(void) { struct P t = {1}; return &t; }
struct P *f(void) { struct P *t = malloc(sizeof *t); t->x = 1; return t; }
struct P *f(void) { struct P a[2] = {{1}, {2}}; return &a[1]; }
questions.explanation: Memory from malloc lives until it is freed, so that pointer stays valid. A local variable, a parameter and a local array all cease to exist when f returns, so the other three functions return dangling pointers.

questions.questionText: Which member declaration, placed inside struct Node { int data; ... };, causes a compile error?
questions.explanation: While its own definition is being read, struct Node is an incomplete type, so it cannot contain a member of itself by value (such a structure would be infinitely large). Pointers to it have a fixed size, so all the pointer forms are valid self-references.

questions.questionText: The structure struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; }; is the typical node of which data structure?
options: A stack stored in an array
questions.explanation: The node holds data and one pointer to the next node of the same type, which is exactly a singly linked list node. A binary tree node needs left and right pointers, and a doubly linked list node needs both next and prev.

questions.questionText: p points to the first node of a singly linked list of struct Node { int d; struct Node *next; }. Which code frees every node without reading memory that has already been freed?
options: while (p) { struct Node *t = p->next; free(p); p = t; }
questions.explanation: The next pointer must be saved before its node is freed. The first two wrong loops both read p->next from a node that has just been freed (and the second never frees the first node); free(p); p = NULL; releases only the first node and leaks the rest.

questions.questionText: Which declaration defines a node suitable for a binary tree?
options: struct T { int key; struct T left, right; };
struct T { int key; struct T *next; };
struct T { int key; struct T *left, *right; };
questions.explanation: A tree node refers to two children of its own type, so it needs two pointers to struct T. Members of type struct T by value are illegal, a single next pointer makes a list node, and int pointers cannot link to other nodes.

questions.questionText: Given struct Student { int roll; char name[20]; float marks; };, which statement correctly allocates heap memory for exactly one struct Student?
questions.explanation: sizeof(struct Student) is the size of the whole record (28 bytes with 4-byte int and float). sizeof(p) and sizeof(struct Student *) are only the size of a pointer, which is too small, and the result of malloc must be stored in a pointer, not in a structure variable.

questions.questionText: On a typical 64-bit compiler with default alignment (char 1, int 4, double 8 bytes, each aligned to its own size), how many bytes does malloc(10 * sizeof(struct R)) request for struct R { char code; double amt; int qty; };?
questions.explanation: code at 0, 7 padding bytes, amt at 8–15, qty at 16–19, then 4 tail padding bytes to reach a multiple of 8: sizeof(struct R) = 24. Ten records need 10 × 24 = 240 bytes (130 ignores all padding, 200 forgets the tail padding).

questions.questionText: After struct P *p = malloc(sizeof *p); the program calls free(p); and then executes p->x = 5;. What is true about that last statement?
options: It is safe: p still holds the same address, so the record is still there
It is a compile error: a freed pointer cannot be used
free(p) set p to NULL, so it always crashes with a NULL dereference
It is undefined behaviour, because p is a dangling pointer after free
questions.explanation: free releases the memory but does not change the value stored in p, so p now dangles. Writing through it is undefined behaviour that the compiler does not detect; setting p = NULL right after free makes such mistakes easier to catch.
